Live oak can sprout easily from a cut stump so the local practice in California is to just lop them off and leave the stump. Over a period of time they send up dozens of new growths that look like a bush. As these grow one by one the smaller ones die off and you end up with about four or five trunks to replace the one you cut. That's how you tell if a "forest" is new growth from acorns or has been previously harvested. If you want a meadow you have to cover the stump with brush from the tree and burn it to prevent regrowth. Live oak is great for firewood but not much else due to crooked growth. The black oak from the same area in Northern California tends to grow straight up before branching out so you get long straight trunks perfect for milling. Seasoned properly and carefully dried under a tarp you get an exceptional wood. Live oak, even if you can get a straight enough trunk will check badly and warps too much so no one has ever been much interested in using it for more than firewood but if you need to, it's ok for some purposes but must be protected from moisture as it easily rots.
